paras: The killings of Ned Roberts and Elijah Anderson were the shootings of two Black levee workers by levee guards in East St. Louis, Illinois, on the night of June 9-10, 1903, a few hours before a flood broke through the city's Illinois Central embankment. According to the most widely reprinted wire report, seven men fired on Roberts after he demanded his pay and threatened to break the dike, and a guard killed Anderson for refusing to work. The two deaths ran as a few lines inside national flood coverage, in two conflicting wire versions and a brief item in the St. Louis Palladium, and no inquest or arrest was reported.

In early June 1903 East St. Louis had spent a week fighting rising water, and thousands of men were working on the levees and embankments when the Illinois Central dike gave way shortly after midnight. Mayor Cook asked the governor of Illinois for state troops to help guard property, and militia were promised.

Two wire accounts described the death of Roberts, a man who had worked on the dike for several days. In a St. Louis dispatch of June 10, Roberts demanded his pay and threatened to break the dike unless he was paid at once, and "Instantly seven men fired on him and the negro fell dead." Some copies of this dispatch said instead that "seven shots" or "several shots" rang out. The second account said Roberts, "employed as a levee builder," was killed by "members of the levee patrol" while attempting to tear down a portion of the dike, an act it attributed to anger at not being allowed to draw his pay at once.

Only the first dispatch reported a second killing: Elijah Anderson, working on the Illinois Central levee, "refused to work and was killed by the guard." The same dispatch noted that a third Black man, given as Theodore Day or Theodore Ray, drowned while trying to rescue people. No report named the men who fired or gave their race.

No report of an inquest, an arrest, or a charge in either killing appears in the coverage. The Palladium's June 13 flood column, which also listed the drowned and lowered the expected death toll, said nothing about who shot Roberts.

White papers from Washington to Colorado carried the shootings within their flood news, beginning with the Alexandria Gazette and the Washington Evening Star on June 10 and continuing in country weeklies a week later. The version naming both men ran in the Beatrice Daily Express, the Durango Semi-Weekly Herald and the Stark County Democrat, which headed it "DEATH FOR DESERTERS." The Durango paper put the killings into its headline: "Two Negroes Shot Dead for Refusing to Work on Levee." The levee-patrol version appeared in the Evening Star, the Providence News, and the Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican, the last under the subhead "Negro Shot Down." Papers in Iowa, Georgia and South Dakota reprinted it on June 11, and two South Carolina weeklies ran it under "NEGRO SHOT DEAD" a week later.

In both white versions the men's alleged conduct, whether a pay demand, a threat to the dike, or a refusal to work, was given as the reason for the shooting without qualification or comment. The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, a Black weekly, reprinted the levee-patrol paragraph under the headline "Negro Shot Dead" without comment. The St. Louis Palladium, a Black weekly, gave the case one sentence in its "Flood Flotsam" column, saying only that Roberts was shot while "in the act of pulling a sack of dirt" from a dike on Tuesday night. Its item named no pay dispute and no shooter, and neither Black paper mentioned Elijah Anderson.

The accounts disagree on what Roberts was doing when he was shot: threatening to break the dike after a pay demand, tearing down part of it, or pulling a sack of dirt from it. Each version describes only the act attributed to Roberts, and none comes from his fellow workers, his family, or a coroner. Anderson's killing rests on the first wire report and its reprints alone.

reader.title: Killings of Ned Roberts and Elijah Anderson
bases: Two Black levee workers were shot by levee guards during flood work, one after a pay demand and one for refusing to work (A2, A4, A7).

Two distinct wire texts and the St. Louis Palladium agree that Ned Roberts was shot dead on an East St. Louis dike before the break (A2, A4, A13); Anderson's killing appears only in the first wire text and its reprints (A2, A11).
